intro/hello: Welcome to the first chapter of the new course. It is about the one idea that everything after it is built on: attention.
intro/y2014: In 2014, a neural network learned to translate English into French, with no grammar rules and no dictionary built in.
intro/two: One recurrent network reads the sentence. A second one writes the translation.
intro/crack: Within months, the design showed a crack. Long sentences came out badly, because everything had to squeeze through one vector.
intro/patch: The patch for that crack was attention: let the writer look back at the sentence, one word at a time.
intro/big: It became the most important idea in this course: the Transformer, and every large language model since, is built from it.
intro/toy: We will tell it with real models: four tiny translators, trained for this chapter on a toy slice of English and French.
intro/french: The French is real French, word for word, except that colors move after their nouns. The black cat becomes luh shah nwar.
intro/plan: First the encoder and decoder, then the bottleneck, then attention, and finally what attention really is: a soft lookup, with queries, keys and values.
encdec/shape: The shape comes straight from the recurrent network chapter: read a whole sequence, then write another one.
encdec/enc: The encoder is an RNN that reads the English sentence, one word at a time.
encdec/emb: Each word comes in as its embedding, a learned list of numbers, and the encoder folds it into its hidden state, h.
encdec/grids: Each little grid is one state: thirty two numbers, after one more word.
encdec/last: Nothing leaves the encoder until the very end. Its last state becomes the context vector, c.
encdec/only: From this moment on, the English sentence is gone. Those thirty two numbers are all the decoder will ever know about it.
encdec/dec: The decoder is a second RNN. It starts from c, and reads a special start token.
encdec/write: At each step it takes the word it wrote last, together with c, and updates its own state, s.
encdec/softmax: A soft max turns its scores into a probability for every French word, and we take the likeliest. Luh, then shah, then nwar.
encdec/feed: Each word it writes is fed back in as its next input.
encdec/stop: It stops when it writes the end token, so it decides the length of the translation by itself.
chain/chain: Writing one word at a time has a neat reading in probability.
chain/chain2: The chance of a whole translation is the chance of its first word, times the chance of the second given the first, and so on.
chain/name: That is the chain rule of probability. Translation is language modeling, with something to talk about.
chain/probs: For our sentence, the decoder gave every word more than ninety nine percent. Multiplied together, the whole translation still gets about ninety nine percent.
chain/log: Training adds up the log of each word's probability. The log turns the product into a sum.
chain/loss: Flip the sign, and you have the loss: the same cross entropy as in a classifier, once per word.
chain/tf: One trick makes training work: the decoder is fed the correct previous word, not its own guess. It is called teacher forcing.
chain/why: Otherwise, one early mistake would derail every word after it.
chain/back: The loss flows backward through the decoder, through c, and into the encoder. One loss trains both networks.
chain/greedy: At test time there is no teacher. We decode greedily; real systems keep a few of the best partial translations at once, called beam search.
bottleneck/crack: Here is the crack. A five word sentence and a forty word sentence both reach the decoder as the same thirty two numbers.
bottleneck/pack: The encoder has to pack the whole sentence into c, in a form the decoder can unpack, in order. The longer the sentence, the more has to fit.
bottleneck/overwrite: Worse, an RNN overwrites its state a little at every step. By the time the last word arrives, the first words have been squeezed the most.
bottleneck/cho: In 2014, Cho and his colleagues measured this on real translation. Quality fell steadily as sentences grew longer.
bottleneck/sutskever: Soots-keh-ver, Vin-yals and Le found that their much bigger network held up better than expected, helped by a curious trick.
bottleneck/reverse: Feed the English sentence in backwards. Then the first English words sit right next to the first French words the decoder writes.
bottleneck/moved: It made training much easier, but the last words are now further apart. The trick shortens some paths; it does not remove the bottleneck.
cliff/toy: Here it is in our toy. For every length from five to forty words, we draw forty random sentences and count how many each model translates perfectly.
cliff/c32: With a thirty two number context, the model is nearly flawless up to a dozen words. Then it falls off a cliff: past twenty five words, it almost never gets one right.
cliff/c64: Double the context to sixty four numbers, and the cliff moves out, past thirty words. But it is still a cliff.
cliff/attn: Now a model with attention. Its decoder state is also only thirty two numbers, and it is perfect at every length.
cliff/why: It never has to hold the sentence in memory. It looks back at it.
cliff/fail: Here is what failure looks like. Eighteen words. The small model gets the start right, then swaps the fish and the cat near the end.
cliff/real: Bah-dah-now and his colleagues drew the same picture for real English and French: the fixed vector models faded with length, and attention held up past fifty words.
attention/idea: In 2014, Bah-dah-now, Cho and Ben-jee-oh let the decoder look back.
attention/keep: The idea is almost embarrassingly simple: keep every encoder state, not just the last one.
attention/bidir: Its encoder reads in both directions, so each state, h j, describes its word in context, with what comes before and after.
attention/three: Then, before writing each word, the decoder does three small things.
attention/score: First, it scores every English word against its own state, s. How useful does this word look, for what I am about to write?
attention/net: The score is a tiny neural network: project s and h j into a shared space, add, squash with tan h, and read off one number. It is called additive attention.
attention/soft: Second, a soft max turns the scores into weights, alpha, that are positive and add up to one: a budget of attention, spread over the sentence.
attention/sum: Third, it reads the weighted average of the encoder states. That is a fresh context, c t, made just for this word.
attention/chat: Here the model is about to write shah. The score for cat towers over the rest.
attention/chat2: The soft max gives it ninety nine percent of the weight, so the context is almost exactly the state for cat.
attention/step: Then the decoder takes its usual step, with c t in place of the one fixed c.
attention/price: The decoder no longer carries the sentence. It only tracks what it has written. The price is one score per English word, for every word it writes.
alignment/rows: Stack the weights for every word the decoder writes, one row each, and you get a picture called the alignment matrix.
alignment/build: Luh looks at the. Shah looks at cat. Then nwar looks back at black. Vwah looks at sees.
alignment/cross: Every color makes a little cross: forward to the noun, then back to the color, as the word order changes.
alignment/nobody: Nobody told the model which words go together; it was only trained to produce the right French. The alignment fell out on its own.
alignment/paper: The original paper shows the same pictures for real sentences.
alignment/eea: In its best known example, European Economic Area becomes zone économique européenne, and the attention runs backwards across the three words.
alignment/end: The last row is the end token. It has no word to look at, so its attention wanders.
alignment/dot: We also trained a model with a simpler, dot product score. Its alignments look almost exactly the same.
lookup/strip: Now take the translation away, and look at what one attention step does all by itself.
lookup/dict: Think of a Python dictionary. You hand it a key, and if that exact key is in there, you get back its value.
lookup/roles: Attention has the same three roles. A query, q: what you are looking for. Keys, k: what each entry is filed under. And values, v: what each entry holds.
lookup/graded: But it relaxes both halves. Matching is graded: every key gets a score against the query.
lookup/blend: And the answer is a blend of every value, weighted by the soft max of the scores.
lookup/picture: Here, five keys are points in a plane, and their values are colors. The background shows what the lookup returns for a query at every spot.
lookup/move: Move the query, and the answer slides smoothly from one color into the next.
lookup/hard: A hard lookup returns only the best match. The plane breaks into flat regions with sharp borders.
lookup/sharp: Sharpen the soft max, and soft turns into hard.
lookup/qkv: In Bah-dah-now's model, the query is the decoder state, and the keys and values are both the encoder states.
lookup/proj: Nothing forces them to be the same. The Transformer computes q, k and v with three separate learned projections.
soft/why: Why blend at all? A hard lookup is cheaper, and a trained model's weights are often nearly all on one word anyway.
soft/line: Here is a lookup on a line: five keys at fixed positions, each holding a number. The query is a position too.
soft/stairs: The hard lookup is a staircase. Move the query a little and the same key still wins, so nothing changes. Then, at a border, it jumps.
soft/flat: Gradient descent needs to know which way is downhill. A flat step says nothing: the gradient is exactly zero.
soft/ramp: The soft lookup is a smooth ramp. Nudge the query, and the output moves a little. There is always a slope to follow.
soft/descend: Ask for a target value and run gradient descent on the query. The soft learner slides right to it. The hard learner never moves.
soft/formula: The gradient of a soft lookup is short enough to read. Raising one key's score pulls the output toward that key's value, in proportion to its weight.
soft/zero: It also says where learning stops. A key with almost no weight gets no gradient. And a key with all the weight already equals the output.
soft/sharp: So a soft max that is too sharp behaves like a hard lookup, and stops learning. Remember that. The Transformer has to guard against it.
scores/luong: Bah-dah-now's score is a small network. In 2015, Loo-ong, Pham and Manning tried simpler ones, and in their experiments the simple ones did as well or better.
scores/dot: The plainest is the dot product: multiply matching entries and add them up. It has no parameters at all.
scores/general: The general form puts one learned matrix between the query and the key.
scores/plane: For a fixed query, the dot product score over all possible keys is a tilted plane. It rises forever in the direction of the query.
scores/bump: The additive score is a little neural network, so it can bend. With the right weights, it peaks on keys near the query.
scores/learned: But the vectors are learned, so the network shapes its keys and queries until dot products mean what it needs.
scores/matmul: And the dot product has a decisive advantage. Stack the queries into a matrix, Q, and the keys into K. One matrix multiply gives every score at once.
scores/three: So attention becomes soft max of Q K transpose, times V: three matrix operations, exactly what GPUs do fastest.
scores/block: The additive score must first build a block of tan h inputs, one for every pair.
scores/size: Its one weakness: it adds one product per dimension, so with hundreds of dimensions the scores grow large and the soft max goes sharp. The next chapter fixes that with one division.
costs/cost: What does attention cost? One score per English word, for every French word. For a sentence, nothing much. For thousands of tokens, it becomes the main cost, and later chapters return to it.
costs/path: In exchange, every word the decoder writes gets a one step path back to every source word. Before, information had to crawl through both recurrences.
costs/left: But attention did not remove the recurrence. The encoder still reads one word at a time, and the decoder still writes one word at a time.
costs/wait: Each step waits for the one before. A GPU cannot spread a sentence across its thousands of cores.
costs/self: The 2017 answer was to let attention do the reading too. Every word attends to every other word in its own sentence. That is called self attention.
costs/drop: Drop the recurrence entirely, and the whole sentence is processed at once. That is the Transformer, the next chapter.
outro/r1: Let's recap. An encoder reads the sentence into one vector, c, and a decoder writes the translation from it.
outro/r2: One vector for every sentence is a bottleneck. Quality falls off a cliff as sentences grow, and a bigger vector only moves the cliff.
outro/r3: Attention keeps every encoder state. For each word it writes, the decoder scores them all, takes a soft max, and reads the weighted average.
outro/r4: Stripped down, that is a soft dictionary lookup. A query is scored against keys, and the answer is a blend of values.
outro/r5: Blending, instead of picking the best match, is what makes it learnable with backprop.
outro/r6: And with dot product scores, all of it is three matrix operations: soft max of Q K transpose, times V. That is where the Transformer begins.
outro/next: Next, open the interactive chapter. The four translators run live in your browser: step through them, break them with long sentences, and drag a query around.
